authoredFrom: BD16 — `source`/`.` is textual inclusion into the CALLING shell's scope, so the relationship is `part_of`, not `imports`. The TARGET is the part's MODULE SYMBOL, never the path: the arbiter resolves target strings against SYMBOL NAMES and has no space for a filesystem path (the cpp lane measured a path target at 0 resolved of 4,612 `part_of` rows), and the symbol this lane publishes for a file is its basename WITH its extension (BD2), so `source ./lib/helpers.sh` targets `helpers.sh`. The written path stays in `metadata.partPath`. `metadata.partRole` is mandatory and is `"library"` on every row: this file carries the directive and names the part. THREE IMPOSTORS are forbidden: `bash x.sh`/`sh x.sh` EXECUTE a file in a new process (never an inclusion — they already publish `calls` edges to the interpreter); an inclusion inside `( … )` or `$( … )` runs in a FORKED shell whose scope this file never sees; a path whose last segment is an EXPRESSION (`source "$lib"`) names no part at all. Whole-corpus denominators (2,962 git-tracked .sh/.bash files, 0 parse failures): 522 `source`/`.` sites -> 470 ELIGIBLE after the two refusals (18 child-process, 34 no-nameable-part) -> 470 `part_of` rows, 1:1, measured by probe-bash-silent-types.mts --corpus and reconciled site-by-site by probe-bash-part-of-sites.mts (census-bash-extended-2962.txt, reconciliation-bash-part-of-2962.txt).

expectRelationships.note: the POSITIVE form: a literal path, its last segment is a name, no child-process boundary.
a path built from a variable is still an INCLUSION whose part is nameable (the last segment is `helper.sh`); the row carries resolution:dynamic exactly as the references row beside it does.
the `.` spelling — bash's second textual-inclusion keyword.
a command substitution in the DIRECTORY part does not stop the LAST segment (`next-to-me.sh`) from naming the part; the row stays honest through resolution:dynamic.

an inclusion INSIDE A FUNCTION is still this shell's scope (a function is not a process), so it fires exactly like a top-level one; the source is the FILE, not the enclosing function, because the directive is the file's.
the MENTION row is unchanged and stays beside the part_of row: this file names that path, which is a different fact from what the file becomes.

the MENTION row of a function-scoped inclusion is owned by the ENCLOSING FUNCTION (the mention is a fact about the scope that names the path), while the part_of row above is owned by the FILE (the inclusion is the file's). The two rows disagree about their source and agree about everything else, which is the BD1 line rule working per fact, not per site.
IMPOSTOR 1, pinned in its honest form: `bash ./lib/child.sh` is a CALL to an interpreter that EXECUTES a file in a new process. It must publish `calls` — and never `part_of` (the forbid row below).

forbidRelationships.note: THE RELABEL: `source`/`.` is `part_of`, not `imports` — the construct imports nothing (the included file's bindings ARE this file's, and it cannot be resolved as a separate module). One forbid row per target shape, so a revert of the relabel fails the fixture no matter which row it re-opens.
the target is the SYMBOL, never the path — the exact defect the cpp lane measured at 0 resolved of 4,612 rows.
IMPOSTOR 1: `bash ./lib/child.sh` / `sh ./lib/child.sh` EXECUTE a file in a new process. An execution is never an inclusion, so no `part_of` row may name the executed file.

IMPOSTOR 2: `( source ./lib/in-subshell.sh )` runs the inclusion in a FORKED shell — the included text shares that child's scope, not this file's, so the single-shared-scope fact `part_of` asserts is FALSE there.
IMPOSTOR 2, command-substitution form: `$(source ./lib/in-cmdsub.sh; echo hi)` forks a shell for the substitution.
IMPOSTOR 3: `source "$lib"` — the path's last segment is an EXPRESSION, so no module symbol can be named at all; the site is recorded as a pattern, never as an edge.
the source is the FILE (the module symbol), never the enclosing function: the directive is the file's, and a function-scoped row would be unresolvable by construction.
